description_full: NVE Corporation develops and sells devices that use spintronics, a nanotechnology relying on electron spin to acquire, store, and transmit information in the United States. The company manufactures spintronic products, including sensors and couplers for use in sensing and transmitting data. Its products comprise standard sensors to detect the presence of a magnetic or metallic material to determine position, rotation, or speed for the factory automation market; and custom and medical sensors for medical devices to replace electromechanical magnetic switches. The company also offers spintronic couplers for power conversion, industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and the Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) markets; DC-to-DC converters for use in energy conversion systems and industrial networks for IIoT and AIoT. Additionally, it undertakes contracts for research and development and licenses spintronic magnetoresistive random access memory technology. The company sells its products through distributors. NVE Corporation was founded in 1989 and is headquartered in Eden Prairie, Minnesota.

financial_summary: NVE Corporation is a small-cap technology business with a $368M market cap on $26M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -12% over the past three years and -1% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 33% against a 10% cost of capital — a 23-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 79% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $14M in free cash flow — roughly 55 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.10× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 5.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
